title: Singleton
summary: Recognize a single shared instance; prefer passing it in over hiding it.

parts.rule: Singleton combines two ideas: only one instance exists in a scope, and code can obtain it through a shared access point. Often you need only the first. Construct one long-lived object at the composition root and inject it, so ownership and dependencies remain visible without a static global.
parts.why: A global getInstance() looks convenient but hides a dependency in every caller, locks tests to shared state, and makes initialization order part of the program's behavior. Explicit lifetime management gives the same resource sharing while allowing a test, worker, or tenant to use a different instance when needed.
parts.example: A service process needs a database pool capped at 20 connections. With Database.getInstance() called from 12 repositories, each repository silently depends on global state. A unit test must reset that global between cases, and parallel tests can change it underneath one another. Instead, main reads configuration once, creates DbPool(maxConnections=20), and passes that reference to UserRepo, OrderRepo, and their services. Production still has one pool, but the type itself does not enforce global access. A repository test passes FakeDbPool with 3 prepared rows; a concurrency test can create two isolated pools without reflection or reset hooks. The composition root also closes the pool during shutdown, making its lifetime explicit. A metrics registry or immutable configuration snapshot can use the same pattern. Be precise about scope: one instance per process still means 8 instances when the service runs in 8 processes, so Singleton does not provide cluster-wide uniqueness. If lazy initialization is unavoidable, the accessor must be thread-safe and failure behavior must be defined, but that solves construction races—not hidden coupling. A domain object such as ShoppingCart must never be a singleton because each request or user needs separate mutable state.
parts.use: Share one instance when a process-wide resource is expensive or represents one lifecycle, such as a connection pool, metrics registry, or configuration snapshot. Prefer having main or a dependency-injection container own it and pass a narrow interface to consumers. State the scope: request, process, tenant, or cluster.
parts.refuse: Do not use a static singleton as the default home for domain services or mutable request data. Avoid global reset rituals in tests and accessors that can initialize in surprising order. If a parent object can simply own a long-lived collaborator, that is lifecycle management rather than a reason to embed the Singleton pattern in the collaborator.

body:
Rule. Singleton combines two ideas: only one instance exists in a scope, and code can obtain it through a shared access point. Often you need only the first. Construct one long-lived object at the composition root and inject it, so ownership and dependencies remain visible without a static global.

Why it matters. A global getInstance() looks convenient but hides a dependency in every caller, locks tests to shared state, and makes initialization order part of the program's behavior. Explicit lifetime management gives the same resource sharing while allowing a test, worker, or tenant to use a different instance when needed.

Worked example. A service process needs a database pool capped at 20 connections. With Database.getInstance() called from 12 repositories, each repository silently depends on global state. A unit test must reset that global between cases, and parallel tests can change it underneath one another. Instead, main reads configuration once, creates DbPool(maxConnections=20), and passes that reference to UserRepo, OrderRepo, and their services. Production still has one pool, but the type itself does not enforce global access. A repository test passes FakeDbPool with 3 prepared rows; a concurrency test can create two isolated pools without reflection or reset hooks. The composition root also closes the pool during shutdown, making its lifetime explicit. A metrics registry or immutable configuration snapshot can use the same pattern. Be precise about scope: one instance per process still means 8 instances when the service runs in 8 processes, so Singleton does not provide cluster-wide uniqueness. If lazy initialization is unavoidable, the accessor must be thread-safe and failure behavior must be defined, but that solves construction races—not hidden coupling. A domain object such as ShoppingCart must never be a singleton because each request or user needs separate mutable state.

[[diagram:one]]

When to use. Share one instance when a process-wide resource is expensive or represents one lifecycle, such as a connection pool, metrics registry, or configuration snapshot. Prefer having main or a dependency-injection container own it and pass a narrow interface to consumers. State the scope: request, process, tenant, or cluster.

When to refuse. Do not use a static singleton as the default home for domain services or mutable request data. Avoid global reset rituals in tests and accessors that can initialize in surprising order. If a parent object can simply own a long-lived collaborator, that is lifecycle management rather than a reason to embed the Singleton pattern in the collaborator.
